newsitem.title: UK: UK's cash-rich BBC seeks further savings.
newsitem.headline: UK's cash-rich BBC seeks further savings.

text.p: The BBC said on Tuesday it had swung from deficit to a positive cash balance of 365 million pounds ($617 million) as it gears up for the launch of new digital television services.
Unveiling the BBC's accounts for 1996/97, director-general John Birt said the state-owned corporation was setting a target of boosting efficiency by a further 20 percent over the next five years.
The BBC plans to invest nine percent of its revenue on its digital strategy and to plough 500 million pounds into its existing network in the coming five years.

The BBC, which derives most of its income from an annual licence fee levy on all television households, has transformed its finances in the 1990s through cost savings and the sale of its transmission network.
Birt said a new five-year licence fee settlement should yield an additional 180 million pounds. The BBC also netted 244 million pounds from the sale in February of its domestic transmission business.

"Together, these decisions were an historic breakthrough for the BBC, a vote of confidence in an organisation whose very nature, scope and survival were being questioned little more than a decade ago," Birt told reporters.
BBC borrowings peaked at 183 million pounds in 1993/94. They have now been eradicated as the corporation saved millions through an assault on what it termed "waste and inefficient practices".

The BBC shed 1,700 domestic staff in 1996/97 -- some eight percent of the total. Birt refused to be drawn on further job cuts but said that a higher proportion of staff would be employed in programme making. Trades unions have criticised Birt in recent days after it emerged that his annual salary rose almost 20 percent to 354,000 pounds last year. But BBC chairman Sir Christopher Bland said the figures were in line with the norm for executives in the media industry.
The BBC plans to launch new free services including a 24-hour news channel next year as Britain introduces digital broadcasting, with its extra channel capacity.
The BBC has also set up a joint venture with pay television operator Flextech Plc to launch UK subscription channels based on the BBC's extensive programme library.

That deal has been concluded by BBC Worldwide -- the corporation's commercial arm. BBC Worldwide had turnover of 354 million pounds in the year to end March and contributed 73.5 million to the corporation's budget, a dip of four percent on 1995/96.
That contribution is small beer compared with licence fee income of 1.9 billion pounds. But the BBC said it remained on target to increase it threefold to 200-250 million pounds over the next decade.
Worldwide last month launched a new Internet service, the fruit of its partnership with computer company ICL, owned by Japan's Fujitsu.
It is also negotiating with Discovery Communications Inc of the U.S. to create a joint venture to sell factual programmes to international markets.

"When the joint ventures with Flextech, ICL and Discovery are fully operational we shall have re-positioned BBC Worldwide for the digital age in the UK and internationally, on screen and on-line," said Bob Phillis, BBC Worldwide chief executive.($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
